title: Guess Number Higher or Lower
description: Brute force to optimized: sequential guessing versus binary search using the guess() API as the three-way comparison.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: A number is picked between 1 and n (inclusive). You must guess it using an API guess(num) that returns -1 if num is higher than the picked number, 1 if num is lower, or 0 if num is exactly the picked number. Return the picked number.

blocks.text: The guess() API gives exactly the same information a direct comparison to a sorted array element would: whether your guess is too high, too low, or exactly right. This makes the problem structurally identical to standard binary search, just phrased as a guessing game.

blocks.title: Analogy: The Classic "Guess My Number" Game
blocks.text: Picture the familiar game where a friend picks a number in a range and tells you "higher" or "lower" after each guess. The optimal strategy is always to guess the middle of the remaining possible range, exactly halving the possibilities every time.

blocks.caption: guess() gives direction feedback, exactly mirroring a sorted-array comparison

blocks.text: Result: 6. Binary search converges on 6 by repeatedly halving the range [1,10].

Before guessing numbers in any arbitrary order, notice that guess() gives exactly a three-way comparison (too high, too low, correct), the same information binary search uses when comparing to a sorted array's middle element, so the identical halving strategy applies directly.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: guess(mid) returning -1 means mid is too high, so the picked number must be smaller, narrowing the search to [lo, mid-1].

Observation 2: guess(mid) returning 1 means mid is too low, narrowing the search to [mid+1, hi].

Observation 3: guess(mid) returning 0 means mid IS the picked number, and the search ends immediately.

Observation 4: This is functionally identical to the standard Binary Search template, with guess() replacing the direct nums[mid] versus target comparison.
This leads to standard binary search over [1, n], using guess(mid) as the three-way comparison to narrow the range each step.
Try numbers 1, 2, 3, ... in increasing order, calling guess() on each, until it returns 0.

items: Starting from 1, call guess(num) for each num in increasing order.
Return the first num for which guess(num) returns 0.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Trying every number in order is simple and guaranteed correct.
This ignores the DIRECTION information guess() provides (too high/too low), wasting most calls.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n) calls to guess() in the worst case.
Space: O(1).
Limitation: the too-high/too-low feedback is exactly the signal binary search needs to eliminate half the remaining range per call, reducing calls to O(log n).

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why sequential guessing wastes information: guess() tells you the DIRECTION of the picked number relative to your guess, information a sequential scan completely ignores.

Applying binary search directly: treat guess(mid) exactly like comparing mid to a hidden sorted value, narrowing [lo, hi] based on the returned direction.

Handling the three return values: -1 (too high) moves hi to mid-1; 1 (too low) moves lo to mid+1; 0 ends the search immediately.

The core idea: standard binary search, with guess() as the comparison function instead of a direct array lookup.
Binary search with lo=1, hi=n. At each step, call guess(mid); if 0, return mid; if -1 (too high), move hi to mid-1; if 1 (too low), move lo to mid+1.

blocks.caption: Binary search using guess() as the three-way comparison, halving the range each step

blocks.text: The guess() API provides exactly the same three-way comparison a sorted array lookup would (less than, equal, greater than), so the standard binary search invariant holds identically: the picked number is always within [lo, hi], and each call correctly halves the remaining range based on the returned direction.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(log n) calls to guess().
Space: O(1).

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "an API gives higher/lower/correct feedback about a hidden value", think: binary search, using that API call as the comparison.

blocks.text: Sequential guessing costs O(n) calls; binary search costs O(log n) calls, both using O(1) space.

Core Idea: call guess(mid); narrow the range based on the too-high/too-low/correct result exactly as with a sorted array comparison.
Time: O(n) for sequential guessing, O(log n) for binary search.
Most Important Observation: any three-way comparison source, not just a literal array, supports binary search's halving strategy.
